procedures.title: Central Line Placement Under Arrest Conditions
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Vascular Access / Circulatory
procedures.subtitle: Femoral-first access during active resuscitation — landmark or ultrasound-guided, without interrupting compressions.
procedures.description: Femoral-first access without interrupting compressions.

blocks.html:
• Cardiac arrest or peri-arrest where peripheral and intraosseous access are inadequate, failed, or unavailable
  • Vasopressor infusion that will run for hours, at doses or concentrations you do not want in a peripheral vein
  • Volume — but only if you place a large-bore introducer sheath. A triple-lumen is worse than a good peripheral for flow (see §03)
  • Anticipated ECPR, transvenous pacing, or a pulmonary artery catheter — access you will need regardless of how this code ends
  • Post-ROSC, when the line placed under compressions needs to become the line you can keep

What it is not indicated for: getting drugs in faster than an IO. An intraosseous line is already running, already works for every arrest drug, and does not require someone to stop resuscitating and start a sterile procedure. Central access during arrest is for the things IO cannot do — sustained pressors, large-bore volume, a pacing wire, a monitoring column.

blocks.title: Below the diaphragm, drugs take longer
blocks.html: A standard 20 cm femoral catheter sits in the iliac vein or low IVC. During CPR, forward flow from below the diaphragm is poor and drug transit to the central circulation is slower than from an upper-body line or a proximal humeral IO. It still works — but every drug gets a 20 mL flush and the leg gets raised. If you have a choice of sites and no reason to avoid the chest, an upper-body line delivers faster.

• A groin you are going to need for ECMO. If ECPR is on the table — even as a maybe — do not put a resuscitation line in the groin the cannulation team wants. Right femoral vessels are conventionally preferred for VA-ECMO cannulation. Use the left groin, or go above the diaphragm. A triple-lumen in the right femoral vein at minute 12 can cost the cannulation at minute 25, and nobody will remember to tell the ECMO team it is there.
  • Vascular injury, graft, or known thrombus at the intended site. A femoral line above a pelvic fracture or an IVC injury delivers drug into the retroperitoneum.
  • Infection or burn over the site — choose another.
  • Subclavian in severe coagulopathy — the site is not compressible. In a coagulopathic bleeding patient, femoral or IJ are the compressible options.
  • Coagulopathy generally is relative, not absolute, in arrest. So is the absence of full sterile barrier. Both are reasons to plan an exchange later, not reasons to withhold access now.

sections.title: Which Catheter — and Why It Is Usually the Wrong One

blocks.html: The kit you grab determines what the line can do. This decision is made before you scrub, and it is frequently made wrong.

rows: 7 Fr triple-lumen, 20 cm
~25–50 mL/min through the distal lumen
Multiple simultaneous infusions, pressors, monitoring. Not volume.
8.5 Fr introducer sheath (“Cordis”), 10 cm
Hemorrhage and volume. Also the conduit for a transvenous pacing wire or a PA catheter.
16 G peripheral, 1.25 in
~200 mL/min
Reference point — it beats a triple-lumen, because flow falls with catheter length and rises with the fourth power of radius.

blocks.html:
Everything else you need:

  • Ultrasound, linear probe, sterile sheath and gel. In arrest this is not an optional refinement — it is the only reliable way to tell artery from vein when there is no pulse and no color difference. Prepare it while you prep the skin, not after.
  • Chlorhexidine, full barrier drape, gown and gloves — use what the situation allows, and document what it did not.
  • Seldinger components: introducer needle, guidewire, scalpel, dilator, catheter, suture or securement device.
  • Saline flushes for every lumen, and a primed extension set.
  • A pressure transducer or a length of sterile IV tubing (for the manometry check — §06).

rows: Femoral — the default
Does not compete with the airway or the compressor. Compressible. Easy landmarks and easy ultrasound. Can be done by one person in a crowded room.
Slower drug transit during CPR. Highest infection rate. May consume the ECMO groin.
Subclavian

Above the diaphragm, so faster drug delivery. Stays out of the way of both the head and the groin. Best long-term infection profile. Landmarks survive when the vein is empty — it is tethered open by surrounding tissue.
Not compressible. Pneumothorax risk in a patient already being ventilated. Chest wall is moving under compressions.
Internal jugular
Above the diaphragm, compressible, excellent ultrasound target.
Directly contests the airway. Head-of-bed is the busiest square meter in the room. Realistic mainly post-ROSC or when someone else fully owns the airway and the bed can be turned over to you.

blocks.html:
The practical rule: during active compressions, femoral — unless ECPR is a possibility, in which case femoral on the left, or subclavian. After ROSC, when the room calms and the bed is yours, the decision reverts to the usual one.

Say out loud which groin you are taking. Two operators independently deciding “femoral” and arriving at the same groin, or the ECMO team arriving to find both groins used, are avoidable and entirely typical failures.

steps.title: Claim the space and set up on the correct side
steps.html: Announce it: “I am taking the left femoral vein.” Sit or kneel at the groin, outside the compressor's arc. Have the whole kit open and the wire loosened from its dispenser before you start — you will not be able to fish for components one-handed with a needle in a vein that is moving with every compression.

steps.title: Find the inguinal ligament, not the skin crease
steps.html: Draw the line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle — that is the inguinal ligament. Puncture 1–2 cm below it. In an obese patient the skin crease can sit several centimeters distal to the ligament and using it as the landmark puts you too low, in the branching femoral vessels. Puncturing above the ligament is worse: that bleed is retroperitoneal, not compressible, and silent.

steps.title: Put the probe on — short axis first
steps.html: Lateral to medial the structures run NAVEL: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics. The vein is medial to the artery. On ultrasound, the artery is round, thick-walled and resists compression; the vein is more oval and collapses. Be warned: in arrest, an empty artery compresses too, and during compressions the vein can transmit pulsation. Do not rely on pulsatility or on blood color — deoxygenated arterial blood in arrest is dark. Use position and wall thickness, and then use the wire (step 7).

steps.title: Prep and drape as fully as the clock allows
steps.html: Chlorhexidine, let it dry if you can, full drape if someone can hand it to you. If a step gets skipped, skip it deliberately and say so — it goes in the note and it sets up the exchange decision later.

steps.title: Needle in at 30–45°, aspirating continuously
steps.html: Aim just medial to the artery, along the vessel's axis, advancing under constant negative pressure on the syringe. Compressions do not stop. Expect the target to move a centimeter with each one — advance between compressions if you can time it, and accept that this is harder than an elective line. Flash is dark and often non-pulsatile even from an artery, because there is no pulse.

steps.title: Drop the angle, thread the wire, and never let go of it
steps.html: Flatten the needle toward the skin before feeding the wire so it turns up the vessel rather than through the back wall. The wire should pass with no resistance at all. A hand is on the wire at every instant from the moment it leaves the dispenser until it is withdrawn — a wire released during chest compressions embolizes. Do not advance more than about 20 cm.

steps.title: See the wire in the vein. This is the step that prevents the disaster.
steps.html: Turn the probe to long axis over the vein and identify the echogenic wire lying inside it. If you cannot see the wire in the vein, you do not have a venous wire. Slide the probe proximally and confirm it stays in the venous channel. Dilation is the point of no return — ten seconds of ultrasound before the dilator is the cheapest insurance in the procedure.

steps.title: Nick and dilate — shallow
steps.html: Scalpel blade against the wire, cutting away from the wire, just through dermis. Then pass the dilator over the wire only far enough to open the tract — typically 2–3 cm. The dilator is a tissue dilator, not a vessel dilator; burying it perforates the posterior wall.

steps.title: Catheter over wire — wire out the hub first
steps.html: Thread the catheter until the wire emerges from the distal hub, then advance it into the vessel. Femoral catheters sit at roughly 20–25 cm at the skin. Remove the wire and confirm it is intact and whole when it is out.

steps.title: Aspirate every lumen, flush every lumen, secure
steps.html: Every port must draw blood back and flush freely. Suture or use the securement device — a line that is only taped will be removed by the transfer to CT. Then announce it: “Left femoral central line is in and working.”

sections.title: Confirming It Is Venous — When Every Normal Clue Has Failed

blocks.html: In arrest, all three of the usual reassurances are unreliable at once.

• Pulsatility: useless. There is no pulse — and compressions make everything pulsatile.
  • Color: useless. Arterial blood in arrest is desaturated and dark.
  • Ease of flow / low resistance: useless. There is no arterial pressure to push back.

What actually works, in order of usefulness during CPR:

  • 1. Ultrasound of the wire, long axis. The definitive bedside test, available before dilation, and the only one that is fully reliable during compressions. Make it a habit, not a tiebreaker.
  • 2. Transduce the needle or catheter. Connect to a pressure transducer and read the waveform. Post-ROSC this is decisive. During compressions it is muddied — compression-generated arterial waveforms can be substantial — but a clearly arterial trace is still an answer.
  • 3. Manometry. Attach sterile IV tubing to the needle hub, fill it, and hold it vertically. A venous column rises a few centimeters and stops; an arterial column climbs and swings. Interpretable post-ROSC; confounded during compressions.
  • 4. Blood gas from the catheter. Slow, and in arrest the arteriovenous difference narrows — a last resort, not a plan.
  • 5. Post-procedure imaging. Chest film for upper-body lines to confirm tip position and exclude pneumothorax. It answers a question you needed answered twenty minutes earlier — useful for documentation and tip position, not for preventing arterial dilation.

blocks.title: If you dilated an artery — leave the catheter in
blocks.html: A large-bore catheter that has been dilated into the femoral or subclavian artery is tamponading its own hole. Pulling it produces uncontrolled arterial bleeding, and in the subclavian position that bleeding is into a space you cannot compress. Leave it in place, leave it clamped, and call vascular surgery or interventional radiology now. This instinct — not to pull — is counterintuitive and has to be pre-loaded, because in the moment every reflex says remove it.

rows: No flash anywhere
Vein is empty and collapsed — the commonest problem in arrest
Use ultrasound to find the vein rather than hunting. Withdraw slowly under aspiration — the back wall is often transfixed on the way in and the flash appears coming out.
Flash obtained, wire will not pass
Bevel against the wall, or needle tip only partly in the lumen
Do not force — forcing dissects. Drop the angle a few degrees, rotate the needle 90°, re-confirm aspiration, retry. If it still won't pass, start over.
Wire passes but resistance partway
Valve, tortuosity, or the wire has gone up a tributary
Withdraw a few centimeters and re-advance. Confirm position on ultrasound. Never push a wire that resists.
Cannot tell artery from vein
Arrest physiology — all the usual discriminators have failed
Ultrasound the wire in long axis before dilating. If you still cannot say, do not dilate.
Bright pulsatile blood after ROSC
Arterial cannulation, unmasked by return of a pulse
If it is a needle — remove and compress 10 min. If it has been dilated and catheterized — leave it in and call vascular surgery.
Catheter in, no blood returns from any port
Tip against a wall, kinked at the skin, or not in the vessel
Withdraw 1–2 cm, reposition the limb, reattempt aspiration. If it flushes but will not draw, treat it as unverified until imaged.
Groin swelling during resuscitation
The line is extravascular, or an arterial puncture is bleeding
Stop infusing through it. Compress. Reassess with ultrasound. A retroperitoneal bleed from a high puncture will not show as groin swelling.
Wire disappeared
Released during compressions — embolized
Do not chase blindly. Immediate imaging and interventional radiology for retrieval.
Sudden hypoxia / hypotension after a subclavian or IJ attempt
Pneumothorax — or tension, under positive pressure
Clinical diagnosis and needle or finger decompression. Do not wait for a film in a deteriorating patient.
ECMO team arrives, both groins used
Nobody said which side they were taking
Preventable only in advance: declare the side, and preserve the right groin whenever ECPR is conceivable.

blocks.html:
• Arterial puncture and arterial cannulation — the defining risk of this procedure in arrest, because every normal discriminator fails simultaneously. Needle punctures compress; dilated catheters do not come out at the bedside.
  • Retroperitoneal hemorrhage from a femoral puncture above the inguinal ligament. Not compressible, not visible, and presents as unexplained shock after an apparently uneventful line.
  • Guidewire embolization — rare, entirely preventable, and specifically more likely here because compressions jostle the operator's hands.
  • Pneumothorax and hemothorax — subclavian and IJ. In a ventilated patient a simple pneumothorax can tension quickly.
  • Air embolism — upper-body lines, especially on chest recoil. Keep the hub occluded.
  • Vessel perforation and cardiac tamponade — from over-advancing a dilator or a stiff wire.
  • Arrhythmia from a wire in the right atrium or ventricle. Irrelevant in arrest; genuinely dangerous peri-arrest. Limit the wire to ~20 cm.
  • Infection — elevated, because barrier precautions were compromised. Femoral is the highest-risk site. Plan the exchange; see §09.
  • Thrombosis — femoral lines in an immobile ICU patient.

• Re-verify the line now that there is a pulse. Transduce it. Draw a gas from it if there is any doubt. A line that was “probably venous” during compressions gets a definitive answer within minutes of ROSC, because the answer is now easy to obtain.
  • Image it. Chest film for any upper-body line — tip at the cavoatrial junction, no pneumothorax. Femoral lines do not need a film for position but do need a documented function check.
  • Flag it as an emergent line, explicitly, in the chart and at handover. Write down which barrier precautions were and were not used. Lines placed without full sterile technique should be removed or replaced as soon as the patient is stable, generally within 24–48 hours — and the only way that happens is if the next team knows.
  • Reassess whether you still need it. The indication was arrest. If the patient now needs only maintenance fluids and a single infusion, the line's risk has outlived its purpose.
  • Tell the ECMO, IR, and surgical teams which vessels are occupied. Access planning downstream depends on it.

See the wire before you dilate. If you take one thing: long-axis ultrasound confirming the wire inside the vein, every time, before the dilator. Everything else in arrest lies to you.

Protect the right groin if ECPR is possible. The line you place in minute 12 can cost the cannulation in minute 25.

If you dilated an artery, do not pull it. The catheter is plugging the hole. Clamp it, leave it, call vascular surgery.

Grab the right kit. A triple-lumen is not a volume line. If you need blood to move, that is an 8.5 Fr introducer — or a short 14 G peripheral, which beats the triple-lumen anyway.

Puncture below the inguinal ligament, judged from bone landmarks, not the skin crease. Above it, the bleed is retroperitoneal and silent.

The vein is empty, so hunt with the probe, not the needle. And watch for the flash on withdrawal — you transfix the back wall more often than you think.

A hand on the wire at all times. Compressions are shaking the field; this is exactly where wires get let go.

Flush hard and raise the leg after every drug through a femoral line during CPR.

An IO already in and working beats a central line you are still placing. Place this line for what only it can do, not for speed.

Say which side you are taking, out loud. Most access collisions are communication failures, not technical ones.

procedures.title: ECMO Cannulation Prep & Activation
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Vascular Access / Circulatory
procedures.subtitle: Peripheral VA/VV cannulation framework, from activation call to first flow — and the timing discipline that drives ECPR outcomes more than technique does.
procedures.description: VA/VV framework from activation call to first flow.

blocks.html:
VA-ECMO

  • Refractory cardiogenic shock
  • ECPR for witnessed arrest with high-quality CPR and a reversible/treatable cause
  • Post-cardiotomy shock
  • Massive PE with hemodynamic collapse
  • Severe hypothermia with cardiac instability (rewarming crossover)

VV-ECMO

  • Severe refractory hypoxemic and/or hypercapnic respiratory failure despite optimized mechanical ventilation and adjuncts (proning, paralysis, inhaled pulmonary vasodilators)

General

  • Bridge to recovery, bridge to durable device/transplant, or bridge to decision

• Unwitnessed arrest or prolonged downtime with no ROSC and poor CPR quality (for ECPR specifically)
  • Irreversible/non-survivable underlying condition
  • Severe pre-existing multi-organ failure incompatible with meaningful recovery
  • Uncontrolled hemorrhage (relative — requires concurrent source control planning)
  • Lack of institutional capability to manage ECMO post-cannulation (relative to transfer feasibility)

• ECMO cannulation kit (arterial and venous cannulae, sized per patient)
  • Ultrasound (vascular access, cannula tip confirmation)
  • Guidewires, dilators, introducer sheaths
  • Circuit primed and de-aired (pump, oxygenator, tubing) per institutional protocol
  • Anticoagulation (heparin) and ACT monitoring capability
  • Fluoroscopy or TEE if available for cannula positioning confirmation
  • Full cannulation team: proceduralist, circuit specialist/perfusion, nursing, airway/code team continuing resuscitation in parallel for ECPR
Peripheral VA cannulation &mdash; general framework

steps.html: Activate ECMO team early — call the moment criteria are anticipated, not once decompensation is complete.
Continue resuscitation (compressions, ventilation, vasopressors) uninterrupted during setup for ECPR cases.
Prime and de-air circuit in parallel with access — do not let circuit prep be the bottleneck.
Obtain venous access (typically femoral vein) via ultrasound-guided Seldinger technique; serially dilate to accommodate venous cannula.
Obtain arterial access (typically femoral artery) via ultrasound-guided Seldinger technique; consider a distal perfusion catheter to mitigate limb ischemia.
Advance venous cannula to the cavoatrial junction; advance arterial cannula per sizing/institutional target.
Confirm cannula position (fluoroscopy, TEE, or venous blood gas from the venous limb as a surrogate) before connecting to circuit.
Connect cannulae to primed circuit, eliminating air at every connection.
Initiate flow at low RPM, titrate up while monitoring hemodynamics, oxygenation, and circuit pressures.
Anticoagulate per protocol once bleeding risk is assessed; establish ACT/anti-Xa monitoring.
Secure cannulae, obtain confirmatory imaging (CXR, or fluoroscopy if not already done), and transition to ICU-level ECMO management.

blocks.title: Activation delay is the single biggest modifiable factor
blocks.html: For ECPR specifically, time from arrest to flow drives outcome more than any technical detail of the cannulation itself — call for activation the moment ECMO becomes a real possibility, not once every other option has failed.

• Limb ischemia distal to arterial cannula — have a distal perfusion catheter plan ready, not as an afterthought
  • Air embolism during cannulation or connection — de-air meticulously at every step
  • Malposition (venous cannula against a wall, arterial cannula too proximal/distal) — confirm before committing flow
  • Bleeding at access sites, worsened once anticoagulated
  • Delayed activation — the single biggest modifiable factor in ECPR outcomes is time from arrest to flow
  • Harlequin syndrome (differential hypoxia) in peripheral VA-ECMO with native cardiac recovery and poor lung function — may require venous cannula repositioning or conversion to VAV

The clock starts at low-flow/no-flow time, not at the decision to cannulate — activate the team the moment ECMO is a real possibility.

Two operators working access sites simultaneously (one venous, one arterial) meaningfully shortens time to flow.

Circuit priming is often the rate-limiting step, not the cannulation itself — get perfusion/circuit specialist moving in parallel from minute one.

Have your distal perfusion strategy decided before you need it, not while a limb is turning white on the table.

procedures.title: Intraosseous Access
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Vascular Access / Circulatory
procedures.subtitle: Proximal humerus, sternal, and tibial sites — the fastest reliable vascular access when peripheral IV attempts have failed or time doesn't allow for them.
procedures.description: Proximal humerus, sternal, and tibial sites.

blocks.html:
• Cardiac arrest, any age, when a peripheral IV is not already running
  • Shock of any cause where access is the rate-limiting step — hemorrhagic, septic, anaphylactic, cardiogenic
  • Two failed peripheral attempts, or a patient in whom you can see at a glance that attempts will fail (burns, IV drug use, obesity, profound vasoconstriction, hypothermia)
  • Status epilepticus, status asthmaticus, hypoglycemia with altered mental status — time-critical drug delivery in a moving target
  • Pre-hospital and austere settings where ultrasound-guided peripheral or central access is not available
  • As a bridge during RSI when you need induction drugs now and the line you have is unreliable

blocks.title: What the 2025 trials actually showed
blocks.html: Two large randomized trials of out-of-hospital arrest — PARAMEDIC-3 and IVIO — found that an IO-first strategy did not improve survival over an IV-first strategy, and PARAMEDIC-3 found lower rates of ROSC in the IO-first arm. This does not make IO a bad route. It means IO is the answer to “I cannot get a vein,” not a shortcut to be reached for reflexively when a vein is available. If a peripheral IV will be in within about 90 seconds, place the IV. If it won't, drill.

Absolute — pick a different bone:

  • Fracture in that bone, at or proximal to the site. Infusate leaks out the fracture; a tibial IO above a tibial fracture perfuses the hematoma, not the patient.
  • Previous IO attempt in the same bone within 48 hours, successful or not. The old cortical hole is a vent — the new line will run straight out of it into the soft tissue. Cross to the other side or another site.
  • Orthopedic hardware, prosthetic joint, or prior surgery at the site (knee replacement, IM nail, shoulder arthroplasty).
  • Infection, burn, or cellulitis over the insertion point. Seeding the marrow through infected skin produces osteomyelitis. Burned skin over an otherwise good site is not an absolute bar in extremis — but choose unburned skin if any exists.

Relative:

  • Osteogenesis imperfecta, osteopetrosis, severe osteoporosis — fragile or sclerotic bone. Osteopetrotic bone may simply not be penetrable.
  • Landmarks you cannot confidently palpate. Body habitus that defeats palpation is a reason to change sites or use ultrasound, not a reason to guess. A blind drill into soft tissue is the commonest cause of a failed IO.
  • Sternal IO: add prior sternotomy, sternal fracture, and small children to the exclusion list.
A powered driver with the wrong needle in it fails exactly like no driver at all.

• Powered driver (battery drill-type) or manual driver. Check the battery indicator at the start of any shift you might need it. A driver that stalls partway through the cortex leaves a needle you must remove and a site you can no longer use.
  • Needle sets — three lengths, and the length is the decision. The color codes below are the widely used EZ-IO convention; confirm against the set in your own kit.
    • 15 mm (pink): 3–39 kg
    • 25 mm (blue): ≥3 kg — the adult tibial default
    • 45 mm (yellow): ≥40 kg, or any site with heavy overlying tissue. The proximal humerus in an adult is a 45 mm needle, always — the deltoid is thicker than people estimate, and a 25 mm needle in a humerus is the single most common cause of an IO that “placed fine” and then infiltrated.
  • Chlorhexidine or whatever prep is within reach. In arrest this is one pass, not a scrub.
  • Extension set with a Luer lock, primed. Prime it — pushing the air column in the tubing into the marrow first is both wasted time and extra pain.
  • Two 10 mL syringes: one of normal saline for the flush, one for aspiration.
  • Preservative-free 2% lidocaine (cardiac lidocaine) for any patient with a pulse and any perception. This is not optional comfort care — see §09.
  • Pressure bag or infusion pump. Gravity through an IO delivers roughly a milliliter a minute. Without pressure you have access that does nothing.
  • Securement dressing (the winged stabilizer in the kit, or a bulky dressing and tape).

blocks.title: The 5 mm rule
blocks.html: Seat the needle through the skin until the tip touches bone, then look at the hub. At least one black depth marking must be visible above the skin. If no line shows, the needle is too short to cross the cortex and still sit in the marrow — swap up a size before you pull the trigger. Checking this takes two seconds and prevents the failure you won't detect until you flush.

rows: Proximal humerus
~5 L/hr
Volume resuscitation; drugs you want centrally fast; awake patients (least painful site)
Displacement with any arm movement — secure the arm to the torso. Not during unmechanized CPR on that side.
Proximal tibia
~1 L/hr
Default in arrest with ongoing compressions; easiest landmarks; pediatrics
Slowest flow. Posterior extravasation is invisible — you must palpate the calf.
Distal femur
~1 L/hr
Infants and small children — wide, flat, forgiving target
Growth plate. Leg must be straight.
Distal tibia
~1 L/hr
Second-choice extremity site; useful when the knee is involved
Thin cortex — easy to go through and through.
Sternum (manubrium)
High
Military/tactical, dedicated device, bilateral extremity trauma
Dedicated device only. Competes with pad and compression placement.

blocks.html:
The default pairing worth committing to memory: humerus for flow and speed to the central circulation, tibia for a moving resuscitation. Humeral flow is roughly five times tibial, and drug transit to the central compartment is faster — which matters for adenosine and for arrest drugs. But the humeral needle sits in a bone attached to a limb that everyone in the room will move, and it dislodges.

In a running code with manual compressions, the tibia is usually the right call: nobody is near it and nothing displaces it. If you place a humeral IO in that setting, tape the arm down across the abdomen and tell the team it is there.

sections.title: Proximal Humerus — The One People Miss

blocks.html: Almost every humeral failure is a positioning failure, and it happens before the drill comes out.

blocks.alt: Proximal humerus intraosseous access in two steps. First, internal rotation: the arm is adducted with the palm on the umbilicus and the elbow pointing backward, which swings the greater tubercle forward into the operator's target line. Second, the angle: the needle enters the most prominent point of the greater tubercle, one to two centimeters above the surgical neck, and is driven at forty-five degrees toward the elbow. A needle driven straight in instead travels medially through the humeral head into the glenohumeral joint space.
blocks.caption: Internal rotation and the 45° caudad angle are the two things that make this line work, and neither is visible once the drill is in your hand. A needle driven perpendicular to the skin travels medially through the head and into the glenohumeral joint — it will stand up convincingly, flush poorly, and infiltrate.

steps.title: Position the arm — this is the procedure
steps.html: Adduct the arm tight to the chest wall, then internally rotate so the palm rests on the umbilicus and the elbow points posteriorly. If you can, have someone hold it. Internal rotation is what swings the greater tubercle anteriorly into your target line and moves it clear of the acromion. Without it you are drilling into the joint capsule or the deltoid.

steps.title: Find the golf ball on the tee
steps.html: Place the heel of your hand on the anterior shoulder and slide your thumb up the anterior humeral shaft. You will feel the shaft narrow — that notch is the surgical neck — and then a broad, round prominence above it. That prominence is the greater tubercle: the ball sitting on the tee. The target is the most prominent point of that ball, roughly 1–2 cm above the surgical neck. If you never felt a narrowing, you have not found the neck, and your landmark is a guess.

steps.title: Angle 45° down and back
steps.html: Enter perpendicular to the surface of the tubercle, which means aiming roughly 45° caudad (toward the elbow) and slightly posteromedial. Straight-in aiming at the ceiling walks you into the joint space. Think of the needle as pointing at the opposite hip.

steps.title: Push to bone, then check the line
steps.html: Push the needle through the skin and soft tissue manually until the tip stops on bone. Now look: at least one black depth line must be showing. In an adult humerus this should be a 45 mm needle. Only then squeeze the trigger.

steps.title: Let the drill do the work — then feel the change
steps.html: Apply steady, gentle axial pressure and let the driver cut. Leaning on it stalls the motor. You are drilling through a thicker cortex than the tibia, so it takes longer and the “pop” is less obvious. The endpoint is a sudden loss of resistance and a change in the driver's pitch as it unloads, or the hub reaching the skin. Stop there. Continuing drives the needle out the far cortex.

steps.title: Uncouple, unscrew, secure
steps.html: Hold the hub and pull the driver straight off — do not let it torque the needle. Remove the stylet by turning counterclockwise. Attach the primed extension set. Then tape the arm to the torso. A humeral IO not secured to the body has an hourly dislodgement rate that makes it unreliable exactly when you stop watching it.

blocks.alt: Proximal tibial intraosseous landmarks, anterior view of the right knee. The tibial tuberosity is the reference bump. The adult target lies two centimeters medial and one centimeter proximal to it, above the tuberosity. The pediatric target lies one centimeter medial and one to two centimeters distal to it, below the tuberosity, so that it stays clear of the open proximal tibial growth plate. The two targets sit on opposite sides of the tuberosity.
blocks.caption: The tuberosity is the reference, not the target. Adult goes proximal to it; a child goes distal — opposite directions, for the one reason shown here. Getting them backwards in a child puts the needle through an open physis.

steps.title: Find the tuberosity, then move off it
steps.html: Run a finger up the shin to the bony bump below the patella — the tibial tuberosity. You are not drilling into it. Adult: about 2 cm medial and 1 cm proximal to the tuberosity, on the flat anteromedial face of the tibia. Child: about 1 cm medial and 1–2 cm distal — distal, to stay clear of the proximal tibial physis. In an infant, one finger-breadth below and medial.

steps.title: Support the knee, don't suspend the leg
steps.html: Put a rolled towel under the knee so it rests in slight flexion on a solid surface. A leg that bounces on the mattress absorbs the drill and turns a clean insertion into a wandering one.

steps.title: Perpendicular — 90° to the flat surface
steps.html: Unlike the humerus, the tibial approach is straight in, 90° to the flat medial surface. Angling drags the needle toward the thin cortex and out the side.

steps.title: Drill to the give
steps.html: The tibial cortex is thin and the pop is distinct — often the first clear tactile landmark a trainee ever gets. Stop at the pop. In a child the cortex is thinner still and the marrow cavity is shallow; a through-and-through insertion is the classic pediatric error. Feather the trigger rather than holding it down.

steps.title: Stylet out, extension on, palpate the calf
steps.html: After the flush, put your hand behind the calf. The tibia extravasates posteriorly where you cannot see it, and the first sign of a failed tibial IO is often a firm posterior compartment rather than a visible bulge.

blocks.html: Alternate sites

Distal femur (pediatric): leg straight, patella identified. Insert 1 cm proximal to the superior border of the patella and 1–2 cm medial to the midline, aiming straight back (slightly cephalad if anything). Wide target, thick marrow, forgiving — a good choice in a small child when the tibia has failed.

Distal tibia: 2 cm proximal to the most prominent point of the medial malleolus, on the flat medial surface, perpendicular. Thin cortex — easy to over-drill.

Sternum: device-specific (FAST1 / FASTResponder and similar), targeting the manubrium about 1.5 cm below the sternal notch via the device's own locating collar. Fixed depth, no freehand angle to judge. Do not improvise a sternal IO with an extremity needle.

sections.title: Confirming You Are in the Marrow

blocks.html: Four checks, in order. Only one of them is decisive.

• 1. The needle stands unsupported. Let go. A correctly seated IO is held rigidly by cortical bone and stands like a flagpole. One that wobbles, leans, or falls is in soft tissue. This is a fast and powerful negative test.
  • 2. Loss of resistance was felt. Corroborative, not proof — in the humerus it can be subtle, and in osteoporotic bone it can be absent entirely.
  • 3. Marrow aspirates. Nice when it happens. Its absence proves nothing — a substantial fraction of correctly placed IOs never yield aspirate, particularly in arrest. Do not pull a good needle because nothing came back.
  • 4. The flush runs without swelling. This is the test that decides. Push 10 mL of saline briskly in an adult (2–5 mL in a child) while watching and feeling the limb. Free flow with no swelling, no boggy tissue, no resistance building under your thumb — you are in. Anything else means stop.

blocks.title: The flush is not a confirmation step — it is part of the insertion
blocks.html: The marrow cavity is a sponge of trabecular bone and fat, not an open tube. Without a forceful flush the space does not open and nothing will infuse afterward, no matter how perfectly the needle sits. The commonest complaint about IO access — “it's in but it won't run” — is nearly always an under-flushed line. Push it hard, and push it again if flow is sluggish.

sections.title: Lidocaine, Pressure, and What Can Go Through It

blocks.html:
Lidocaine — the sequence matters more than the dose. The saline flush into a conscious patient's marrow is described by patients as among the worst pain in medicine. Lidocaine must go in before the flush, not after.

  • Adult: preservative-free 2% lidocaine, 40 mg (2 mL) slowly over about 120 seconds → let it dwell 60 seconds → flush 5–10 mL saline → a further 20 mg (1 mL) over 60 seconds.
  • Pediatric: 0.5 mg/kg, max 40 mg, same dwell-then-flush sequence.
  • Repeat doses are appropriate for ongoing pain during infusion. Account for the total in any systemic lidocaine ceiling.
  • This is for any patient with a pulse and any plausible perception. It is not indicated in arrest — and if they wake up, give it then.

Pressure. Gravity produces roughly 1 mL/min through an IO. Every infusion that needs to be fast needs a pressure bag at 300 mmHg or a pump. If a resuscitation is running slowly through an IO, check the pressure bag before you blame the needle.

What can go through it: everything. Crystalloid, blood and all components, vasopressors, induction and paralytic agents, antibiotics, TXA, sodium bicarbonate, hypertonic saline, contrast for CT. Onset and peak levels approximate IV. There is no drug class that is IV-only. The proximal humerus is preferred for adenosine and other agents whose effect depends on a tight, fast bolus.

Labs from the aspirate: the first aspirate can be sent for type and screen, chemistry, lactate and blood gas, and correlates acceptably for most. It is unreliable for platelet and white cell counts, and marrow will clog an automated analyzer. Call the lab and the blood bank before you send it — some will not accept it, and you need to know that before it is the only sample you have.

rows: Needle bounces off, drill bogs down
Leaning on the driver and stalling the motor; or a dead battery; or sclerotic bone
Ease the axial pressure and let it cut. Swap batteries. If two attempts stall, change sites.
Drove it in, no pop, hub at skin
Needle too short — it never crossed into marrow
Remove. Re-site on the other limb with the next size up. Do not redrill the same bone.
Needle wobbles / falls over
In soft tissue, or through-and-through out the far cortex
Remove and re-site on a different bone. Hold pressure.
No marrow aspirate
Normal — common in low-flow states
Ignore it. Confirm with the flush instead.
Flush meets hard resistance
Tip against cortex, or the lumen is plugged with a marrow core
One firm attempt to clear. If still blocked, it is a failed line — remove.
Limb swells / calf firms up on flush
Extravasation
Stop immediately. Remove. New site on a different bone. Mark the limb and reassess for compartment syndrome hourly.
Ran fine, then stopped
Dislodgement (classically humeral, with arm movement), or clotting from an inadequate initial flush
Re-flush firmly. Check the needle is still rigid. If it now wobbles, it has moved — replace it.
Correct position but flow is slow
Running on gravity
Pressure bag to 300 mmHg, or a pump. Re-flush.
Awake patient screams on infusion
Lidocaine omitted, or given after the saline flush
Stop the infusion. Give lidocaine, dwell 60 seconds, then restart.
Second IO in the same bone won't hold pressure
The earlier cortical hole is venting the marrow space
Expected and unfixable. Use a different bone — this is why the 48-hour rule exists.

blocks.html:
• Extravasation → compartment syndrome. The complication that matters, and it is essentially always a recognition failure rather than a technique failure. The tibia is the highest-risk site because leakage tracks posteriorly and stays invisible. Any IO limb gets a documented baseline and scheduled re-checks while it is running.
  • Through-and-through penetration — classically the pediatric tibia, from holding the trigger through the marrow cavity and out the far cortex. Presents as a needle that stands but will not flush.
  • Fracture — excess force in osteoporotic or pediatric bone, or a manual needle levered sideways.
  • Osteomyelitis — well under 1%, and rises with dwell time and with insertion through non-prepped or infected skin.
  • Growth plate injury — the reason pediatric tibial landmarks sit distal to the tuberosity and femoral landmarks sit proximal to the patella.
  • Fat and marrow embolization — demonstrable, but not associated with clinically meaningful harm in humans. It is not a reason to withhold or under-flush an IO.
  • Skin necrosis from vesicant or vasopressor extravasation into soft tissue — a downstream consequence of a missed infiltration, not a separate event.

24 hours is the ceiling under most manufacturer instructions, and sooner is better. IO is a bridge. Once the patient is stabilized and a peripheral or central line is in, the IO comes out — leaving it “just in case” accumulates infection risk for access you are not using.

Removal: attach a Luer-lock syringe to the hub (a slip-tip will pull off). Rotate clockwise while drawing straight out along the needle's axis. Do not rock, lever, or bend. Side-loading can shear the needle and leave a fragment in the bone — a problem that becomes an orthopedic consult. Dress the site; it will ooze a little.

Document: site, needle size, time in, time out, lidocaine given, and the limb assessment. If the patient goes to CT or the OR, tell the receiving team the IO is there — humeral needles under a gown are easy to miss and easy to knock out.

Flush like you mean it. If you remember one thing: the marrow cavity does not open until you force it open. Almost every “the IO doesn't work” complaint is an under-flushed line.

The needle stands up or it isn't in. Letting go of the hub is a free, instant, highly specific test, and it is the one people skip in a hurry.

No aspirate is not a failure. More correctly placed IOs yield nothing back than most clinicians expect. Confirm with the flush, not the syringe.

The humerus needs the long needle and the right rotation. Hand on the belly, 45° toward the elbow, 45 mm needle. Get those three and the humerus is the best line in the room; miss any one and it fails quietly.

Secure the arm. A humeral IO not taped to the torso will be pulled out by someone doing something reasonable.

Pressure bag, every time. Access without pressure is not resuscitation.

Never re-drill the same bone. Within 48 hours, the previous hole vents everything you put in. Cross to the other side.

IO is not a second-class line. Every drug, blood product, and contrast agent that goes IV goes IO. Treat it as full access — and then replace it within 24 hours.

American Heart Association. 2020 Guidelines for CPR and ECC — Adult and Pediatric Advanced Life Support: vascular access. Circulation. 2020;142(16_suppl_2).
Roberts JR, Custalow CB, Thomsen TW, eds. Roberts and Hedges' Clinical Procedures in Emergency Medicine and Acute Care, 7th ed. Elsevier; 2019 — Intraosseous Infusion.

Teleflex. EZ-IO Intraosseous Vascular Access System — Instructions for Use. Manufacturer labeling for needle sizing, lidocaine protocol, and dwell time. Confirm against the device stocked in your own institution.

procedures.title: Junctional Tourniquet Application
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Hemorrhage Control
procedures.subtitle: Hemorrhage control at the junctional zones — groin, axilla, pelvis — where a standard limb tourniquet has no purchase.
procedures.description: Hemorrhage control at groin, axilla, pelvis.

blocks.html:
• Life-threatening hemorrhage in a junctional zone — the groin and inguinal region, the axilla and shoulder girdle, the gluteal region, the perineum, and the base of the neck. Anatomy where there is no cylindrical limb for a standard tourniquet to squeeze.
  • Traumatic proximal amputation — a high thigh or shoulder-level amputation leaves no residual limb above the injury to place a limb tourniquet on
  • Junctional bleeding that continues despite correct wound packing and sustained direct pressure
  • As a bridge while a limb tourniquet is converted, or while proximal surgical control is arranged
  • Abdominal aortic occlusion (specific devices only) as a non-invasive analogue of Zone 3 REBOA in pelvic and high junctional hemorrhage

• None absolute in life-threatening junctional hemorrhage.
  • Bleeding a limb tourniquet can reach. If there is a cylinder of limb above the wound, use a standard tourniquet — it is faster, better understood by everyone downstream, and does not require the specific device knowledge these do.
  • Pelvic fracture, for abdominal aortic compression devices. An inflatable wedge pressed onto a disrupted pelvis can displace the fracture and is generally avoided; a pelvic binder plus a groin-targeted device is the better combination.
  • Abdominal aortic occlusion in penetrating abdominal trauma or suspected abdominal injury — you are compressing bowel and a possibly injured aorta against the spine.
  • Pregnancy, for abdominal devices.
  • Any device you have not used before, if manual pressure is working. A fist held correctly on the femoral artery beats forty seconds spent reading a label.
Unlike limb tourniquets, these share almost no technique. This table is the reason this entry exists.

rows:
CRoC
Combat Ready Clamp
A rigid C-clamp bolted to a base plate, driving a pressure disc down onto the vessel by a threaded handle
Inguinal; axilla with repositioning
Needs a firm surface under the patient. Slow to assemble. Very effective once seated, and the pressure is directly and continuously adjustable.

JETT
Junctional Emergency Treatment Tool
A belt with two screw-down pressure pads
Bilateral inguinal simultaneously
The only common device designed for both groins at once — the reason it exists is bilateral proximal amputation. Not for axilla.
SAM Junctional TQ
Pelvic belt with an inflatable Target Compression Device (one or two)
Inguinal, axillary; the belt doubles as a pelvic binder
Inflate to hemorrhage control. Cleared for up to 4 hours. The dual-purpose pelvic function is genuinely useful in blunt trauma.

AAJT-S
Abdominal Aortic and Junctional TQ
Inflatable wedge over the abdomen compressing the aorta against the spine
Distal aorta (at the umbilicus); also axilla and groin
Abdominal application is limited to about 60 minutes — this is whole-body distal ischemia, functionally non-invasive Zone 3 REBOA. Avoid with pelvic fracture, abdominal injury, or pregnancy.

blocks.title: Know the device in your bag, today
blocks.html: Limb tourniquets are close enough to one another that skill transfers. These do not. A CRoC and an AAJT share no motions, no landmarks, and no endpoints. The failure mode is specific and predictable: an operator meets an unfamiliar device during the two minutes it was bought to save, and reads the instructions while the patient exsanguinates. Find out which one your service stocks and put your hands on it before you need it. If you are improvising because you don't know the device, go back to a fist on the ramus.

sections.title: Before the Device: the Things That Work Immediately

blocks.html:
Every junctional device takes time to deploy. The bleeding does not pause for it, so something has to hold the line first — and these techniques are not a lesser substitute, they are the opening move.

  • A fist, a knee, or a heel on the femoral artery. Press at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament — halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle — driving straight down so the artery is compressed against the superior pubic ramus. Use body weight through a straight arm or a knee. This works, it works instantly, and it holds while everything else is organized. It is also exhausting, so rotate people.
  • Pack the wound at the same time (see the wound packing entry). Packing and a junctional device are complementary: the pack controls what is bleeding in the wound, the device controls inflow from above. A device applied over an unpacked cavitating wound often fails.
  • Axillary compression — push the axillary artery against the humeral head, or reach higher and compress the subclavian downward behind the clavicle against the first rib.
  • Abdominal aortic compression by fist — a closed fist or the heel of the hand pressed hard just left of the umbilicus, directed posteriorly toward the spine, with the operator's weight over it. A crude and short-lived measure that can buy minutes in catastrophic pelvic or high groin bleeding.
  • Analgesia. All of this is savagely painful. Ketamine, early.

steps.title: Manual pressure first, and keep it there
steps.html: One person holds the femoral artery against the pubic ramus and does not let go until the device is tightened and has taken over. Deploying a device while nobody is compressing means the patient bleeds throughout the assembly.

steps.title: Expose fully and pack the wound
steps.html: Cut the clothing away to bare skin — a pad over fabric slides. Pack the wound cavity firmly while pressure is maintained proximally.

steps.title: Place the pad over the artery, not over the wound
steps.html: The target is proximal inflow: the femoral artery at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, where it can be pressed onto the superior pubic ramus. This is the single most common misapplication — the pad is instinctively centered on the injury, which compresses a hole rather than the vessel feeding it. Find the landmark by bone, not by the wound.

steps.title: Anchor the belt around the pelvis and tension it
steps.html: Belt-based devices need a firm circumferential anchor before the pad can generate force. Seat the belt, remove the slack, then apply pressure through the pad.

steps.title: Tighten to hemorrhage control — that is the endpoint
steps.html: Screw down, ratchet, or inflate until bleeding stops. Unlike a limb tourniquet, you cannot rely on loss of a distal pulse: the collateral circulation around the pelvis and shoulder is rich, and a palpable distal pulse does not mean the device has failed. Watch the wound, not the foot.

steps.title: Verify after every movement
steps.html: Recheck after each log-roll, lift, and transfer. These devices slip — they sit on a mobile, conical, blood-slick surface, and a pad that has migrated a couple of centimeters off the artery is doing nothing while looking correct.

steps.title: Write the time on the patient
steps.html: On the skin and on the device, in marker. Say it at handover. Ischemic time drives every downstream decision and is the number most often lost.

blocks.html:
Harder than the groin, and less often practiced. The axillary artery has no convenient flat bone beneath it and the shoulder girdle is mobile.

  • Target the axillary artery against the humeral head with the arm adducted, or reach proximally and compress the subclavian artery downward behind the clavicle onto the first rib.
  • Anchor over the opposite shoulder — axillary applications need a counter-anchor across the torso, because there is no circumference to grip. A belt that simply encircles the chest will ride.
  • Pack the wound as well, always. Axillary bleeding has substantial collateral supply through the scapular anastomosis, and inflow control alone often leaves brisk back-bleeding.
  • Watch the airway and breathing. A device anchored across the chest restricts ventilation, and high axillary wounds are close enough to the pleura that a pneumothorax should be actively excluded.
  • Brachial plexus injury is a real consequence of sustained axillary compression. It is accepted in exchange for survival, and it is documented.

sections.title: Abdominal Aortic Occlusion — and Its Clock

blocks.html:
An inflatable wedge placed over the abdomen at the level of the umbilicus, compressing the infrarenal aorta against the vertebral column. Functionally a non-invasive Zone 3 REBOA: it stops inflow to the pelvis and both legs without any vascular access at all.

  • Indication: catastrophic pelvic, perineal, or high bilateral groin hemorrhage not controllable by any other means.
  • Do not use with pelvic fracture, suspected abdominal injury, penetrating abdominal trauma, or pregnancy.
  • Time limit is approximately 60 minutes, and it is a hard limit. Everything below the device is ischemic from the moment it is inflated, and the reperfusion load on release is the same problem REBOA has: potassium, acid, and vasoplegia arriving at once.
  • Announce the clock the way you would for a balloon. Inflation time called out loud, repeated every five minutes, written down.
  • Prepare for release exactly as for REBOA deflation — blood running, pressors connected, calcium drawn up, and a surgeon present. Release gradually, not by opening the valve.
  • Confirm effect by loss of femoral pulses bilaterally and a rise in proximal blood pressure. If neither happens, the device is malpositioned or under-inflated — or the bleeding is above it.

rows: Device on, still bleeding briskly
Pad centered on the wound instead of on the proximal artery
Move the pad to the bony landmark — midpoint of the inguinal ligament, onto the ramus. Check this before anything else.
Still bleeding, pad correctly placed
Insufficient pressure, or the wound cavity is bleeding independently
Increase pressure to the device's limit. Pack the wound if you have not. Reassess for a second site.
Bleeding controlled, then restarts
Device migration — almost always after a move
Re-seat and re-tension. Re-verify after every transfer, every time.
Distal pulse still present
Normal — collateral flow around the pelvis and shoulder
Not a failure. The endpoint is a dry wound, not an absent pulse. Do not over-tighten chasing the pulse.
Device will not seat / keeps sliding
Applied over clothing, or blood-slick skin, or no firm surface beneath
Strip to skin and dry it. Rigid clamp devices need a hard backboard under the patient.
Patient fighting, unmanageable
Pain — these are excruciating
Ketamine. An incompletely applied device because the patient could not tolerate it is a preventable failure.
Bilateral groin wounds, one device
Only JETT covers both simultaneously
Manual pressure on the second side, or a second device. Do not let one side go untreated while perfecting the other.
Abdominal device on, pressure unchanged
Under-inflated, malpositioned — or bleeding above the level of occlusion
Inflate further and confirm both femoral pulses are gone. If still no response, look above the diaphragm.
Collapse when the device comes off
Reperfusion washout
Re-apply. Calcium, product, pressors. Release slowly and only with a surgeon present.
Nobody knows when it went on
Time not recorded
Preventable only up front — marker on skin, spoken at handover, written in the note.

blocks.html:
• Ischemia distal to compression, scaling with dwell time — and with abdominal application, that means the pelvis, both legs, and the pelvic viscera.
  • Reperfusion injury on release — hyperkalemia, acidemia, vasoplegia, arrhythmia and arrest. Identical in kind to REBOA deflation, and prepared for the same way.
  • Compartment syndrome of the compressed limbs after reperfusion. Serial checks; low threshold for fasciotomy.
  • Nerve injury — femoral nerve in the groin, brachial plexus in the axilla. Frequently accepted deliberately.
  • Pressure necrosis of skin and underlying soft tissue at the pad.
  • Bowel injury and aortic injury from abdominal compression, particularly in an already injured abdomen.
  • Ventilatory restriction from abdominal or thoracic-anchored devices.
  • Fracture displacement where a device is applied over an unstable pelvis.
  • Incomplete control creating false reassurance — a device that is on and visible is easy to mistake for a problem solved.

• Name the device. The receiving team may never have seen it. “Junctional tourniquet” is not enough information to release one safely.
  • Give the application time — written on the patient, not only spoken.
  • Say what is packed underneath, and how many rolls or sponges.
  • Say what has already failed, so nobody repeats it.
  • These come off in an operating room, with proximal control obtained and the team ready for reperfusion — not in a resuscitation bay to see whether the bleeding has stopped.
  • For abdominal aortic devices, state the clock as a deadline, not as an elapsed time: “inflated at 14:32, off by 15:32.”

A fist on the ramus works right now. Start there, keep it there, and let the device take over — never the other way around.

The pad goes on the artery, not on the wound. Find it by bone: midpoint of the inguinal ligament, onto the superior pubic ramus.

Pack the wound too. Inflow control and cavity control are different problems and you usually have both.

The endpoint is a dry wound, not an absent pulse. Collateral flow means the pulse can persist with the device working perfectly.

Know your device before the day you need it. Nothing transfers between a CRoC, a JETT and an AAJT except the intent.

Re-check after every move. These slip, and a slipped device looks applied.

Abdominal aortic occlusion has a one-hour clock — treat it exactly like a Zone 3 balloon, including how you come off it.

Give ketamine.

Write the time on the skin.

Kotwal RS, Butler FK. Junctional hemorrhage control for tactical combat casualty care. Wilderness Environ Med. 2017;28(2S):S33–S38.
Kragh JF, Dubick MA, Aden JK, et al. U.S. military use of tourniquets from 2001 to 2010. Prehosp Emerg Care. 2015;19(2):184–190.

procedures.title: Lateral Canthotomy
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Cardiac / Neuro
procedures.subtitle: Emergent decompression of orbital compartment syndrome — a vision-saving procedure with a narrow therapeutic window.
procedures.description: Vision-saving orbital compartment decompression.

blocks.html:
• Orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar hemorrhage or rapidly expanding orbital process, typically presenting with proptosis, decreased visual acuity, elevated intraocular pressure, and an afferent pupillary defect
  • Clinical diagnosis with a time-critical window — permanent vision loss can occur within approximately 90-120 minutes of sustained elevated intraocular pressure

• None absolute given the time-critical, vision-threatening nature of true orbital compartment syndrome
  • Globe rupture — canthotomy technique should be adapted with caution, avoiding any additional pressure on the globe itself; some sources still support proceeding if compartment syndrome is confirmed, but extra care is warranted

• Local anesthetic with epinephrine
  • Straight (Mayo/suture) scissors
  • Toothed forceps
  • Hemostat (for the crush technique on the lateral canthal tendon prior to cutting, optional but reduces bleeding)

steps.html: Confirm the clinical diagnosis: elevated intraocular pressure, proptosis, decreased vision, in the setting of trauma or rapid orbital swelling.
Infiltrate local anesthetic with epinephrine at the lateral canthus.
Using a hemostat, crush the lateral canthal tendon area for several seconds to reduce bleeding (optional step, improves hemostasis).
Using straight scissors, perform a lateral canthotomy — a horizontal incision through the lateral canthus, extending from the lateral commissure toward the orbital rim.
Identify the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon by palpating/pulling the lower lid laterally with forceps.
Cut the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon (cantholysis) — this is the step that actually releases the compartment pressure; the canthotomy incision alone is often insufficient.
Reassess intraocular pressure and visual function after cantholysis; if inadequate improvement, consider releasing the superior crus as well.
Arrange urgent ophthalmology follow-up/consultation regardless of immediate improvement.

blocks.title: The canthotomy incision alone is not the therapeutic step
blocks.html: Cutting the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon (cantholysis) is what actually relieves compartment pressure — stopping after the skin incision is a common technical error that leaves the orbit undecompressed.

• Performing the canthotomy incision alone without cantholysis — this is a common technical error and does not adequately decompress the orbit
  • Bleeding at the incision site
  • Inadequate pressure relief requiring release of the superior crus as well
  • Delayed recognition/intervention — the biggest driver of permanent vision loss is time, not technical difficulty of the procedure itself

The canthotomy is not the therapeutic step — the cantholysis (cutting the inferior crus of the tendon) is what actually relieves the compartment pressure. Don't stop after the skin incision.

This procedure is time-critical in a way few others in this library are — roughly a 90-120 minute window before vision loss becomes permanent, so recognition speed matters as much as technique.

Reassess after the inferior crus release; if pressure and proptosis haven't adequately improved, proceed to the superior crus without hesitation.

items.html: Vassallo S, Hartstein M, Howard D, Stetz J. Traumatic retrobulbar hemorrhage: emergent decompression by lateral canthotomy and cantholysis. J Emerg Med. 2002;22(3):251-256.
Roberts JR, Custalow CB, Thomsen TW, eds. Roberts and Hedges' Clinical Procedures in Emergency Medicine and Acute Care, 7th ed. Elsevier; 2019 — Lateral Canthotomy chapter.

procedures.title: Massive Transfusion Protocol Activation & Sequencing
procedures.kicker: The Critical Vector · CRISIS · Hemorrhage Control
procedures.subtitle: Getting blood products moving before the lab catches up — ratio-based transfusion as a bridge to definitive hemorrhage control.
procedures.description: Ratio-based transfusion sequencing and logistics.

blocks.html: The protocol exists to be pulled early. Over-activation costs product; under-activation costs the patient.

Activate on any of these — do not wait for a lab value:

  • Critical Administration Threshold (CAT+): ≥3 units of red cells in any 60-minute period. This is the most useful real-time trigger — it is the one you can recognize while it is happening.
  • ABC score ≥2 (one point each): penetrating mechanism · SBP ≤90 · HR ≥120 · positive FAST.
  • Shock index (HR ÷ SBP) >1.0, and especially >1.4.
  • Anticipated ≥10 units in 24 h or ≥4 units in 1 h — the classic definitions, useful for audit, too slow to be a bedside trigger.
  • Clinical gestalt. A ruptured AAA, a mangled pelvis, a boggy uterus that will not contract, or bright blood filling a chest tube is enough. Pulling the trigger on a patient who turns out not to need it is a recoverable error.

Non-trauma activations matter just as much: obstetric hemorrhage, upper GI variceal bleeding, ruptured aneurysm, and post-operative surgical bleeding all belong here.

• None absolute in the presence of major hemorrhage.
  • Documented refusal of blood products. Follow the patient's stated wishes and your institution's policy. Have the alternative plan ready before you need it — cell salvage, TXA, fibrinogen concentrate, factor concentrates, and aggressive surgical control. Know which of these an individual patient does and does not accept; the categories are not uniform.
  • Uncontrolled surgical bleeding is not a transfusion problem. Product buys time to get to the OR, angiography suite, or the balloon. If activation is being used as a substitute for source control, the protocol will fail no matter how well it is run.
  • Futility. Massive transfusion in a patient with unsurvivable injury consumes a finite regional blood supply. This is a judgment call made early and explicitly, not one drifted into.

• The activation mechanism itself — one phone number or one order. Know it before the day you need it. The commonest delay in a massive transfusion is not the blood bank; it is the four minutes spent working out who to call.
  • Rapid infuser with integrated warmer (Belmont, Level 1, or equivalent) — capable of 500–1000 mL/min at 38 °C. A blood warmer on a gravity line is not a rapid infuser.
  • Two large-bore access points. Flow scales with the fourth power of radius and inversely with length: a short 14–16 G peripheral outperforms a long triple-lumen central line for volume. If central access is needed, use an introducer sheath (8.5 Fr), not a multi-lumen.
  • Forced-air warmer, warmed room, warmed fluids — hypothermia is generated by the resuscitation itself.
  • Point-of-care testing: blood gas with ionized calcium, lactate, hemoglobin; and viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) if available.
  • A whiteboard and a scribe. Product counts, time of activation, and calcium doses are all lost in real time without someone writing them down.
Ratios are prescribed so nobody has to calculate during the event.

rows: Red cells
6 units
Uncrossmatched O to start. O-negative for females of childbearing potential; O-positive is acceptable for males and post-menopausal females and protects a scarce O-neg supply.
Plasma (FFP / thawed)
6 units
Thawing takes 20–30 min unless pre-thawed plasma is stocked — this is the usual reason pack 1 arrives red-cell-heavy.
Platelets
1 apheresis unit
One apheresis unit ≈ 6 pooled units — this is what makes a 6:6:1 pack a “1:1:1” ratio. Miscounting this is how platelets get under-given.
Cryoprecipitate
Often not in pack 1
Must usually be asked for. See §06 — fibrinogen falls first and is the thing most often missed.
Whole blood (LTOWB)
Increasingly pack 1
Low-titer group O whole blood delivers the balanced ratio in a single bag with one venipuncture-equivalent of dilution. Where stocked, it is the simplest way to get the ratio right.

blocks.html: What PROPPR actually showed. 1:1:1 versus 1:1:2 produced no difference in 24-hour or 30-day all-cause mortality. What it did show: more patients achieved anatomic hemostasis, and fewer died of exsanguination in the first 24 hours, with 1:1:1. That is the basis for the default — a reasonable empiric starting ratio, not a proven mortality intervention. It is a bridge to goal-directed therapy, and should be abandoned for viscoelastic guidance as soon as you have data.
Pediatric dosing

• Red cells: 10–20 mL/kg per round
  • Plasma: 10–20 mL/kg
  • Platelets: 10–15 mL/kg
  • Cryoprecipitate: 5–10 mL/kg
  • Pediatric massive transfusion is commonly defined as >40 mL/kg of any product in 24 h, or >half the estimated blood volume in 3 h.
  • Children tolerate the citrate and potassium load of rapid transfusion worse than adults, not better. Calcium and potassium need checking sooner.

sections.title: Drugs That Go With the Blood

blocks.html: These are the doses. They are forgotten more often than the blood is.

rows: Tranexamic acid — trauma
1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h
Within 3 hours of injury. Beyond 3 hours CRASH-2 showed a signal of harm — check the clock, not just the bleeding. Rapid push causes hypotension.
Tranexamic acid — postpartum
1 g IV over 10 min; repeat 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 min or restarts within 24 h
WOMAN trial. Same 3-hour window from onset of bleeding.
Tranexamic acid — pediatric
15 mg/kg (max 1 g) over 10 min, then 2 mg/kg/h
Extrapolated dosing; confirm locally.
Calcium chloride 10%
1 g (10 mL) = 13.6 mEq elemental Ca

Roughly 1 g per 4 units of product, or empirically with pack 1. Three times the elemental calcium of gluconate per gram. Sclerosant — prefer a central or large vein, but do not withhold it for that reason in exsanguination.
Calcium gluconate 10%
3 g (30 mL) = 13.6 mEq elemental Ca
Peripheral-friendly equivalent. Requires hepatic metabolism to liberate calcium — less reliable in the shocked, acidotic liver.
Calcium — pediatric
CaCl 20 mg/kg or Ca gluconate 60 mg/kg
Same trigger: ionized calcium, or empirically per pack.
Fibrinogen (cryoprecipitate)
10 pooled units (raises fibrinogen ~50–100 mg/dL)
When fibrinogen <150 mg/dL, or <200 in obstetric hemorrhage. See §06.
Fibrinogen concentrate
Where stocked — no thaw time, no ABO matching, smaller volume.
Anticoagulant reversal
Agent-specific
Ask about DOACs and warfarin on every bleeding patient. Reversal is a separate decision tree — see the anticoagulant reversal protocol; do not improvise doses here.

blocks.title: Hypocalcemia is the fourth point of the diamond
blocks.html: Every unit of product carries citrate, which chelates ionized calcium. Ionized calcium <0.9 mmol/L on arrival independently predicts mortality and the need for massive transfusion. Calcium is required for platelet function and for nearly every step of the coagulation cascade — you cannot clot without it, and no amount of plasma substitutes for it. It is also negatively inotropic when low. Give calcium with the first pack and recheck the ionized level every 30 minutes; target >1.1–1.2 mmol/L.

rows: Ionized calcium
>1.1–1.2 mmol/L
<1.1 — and empirically with pack 1 regardless
Fibrinogen
>150 mg/dL (>200 obstetric)
<150 → cryoprecipitate or concentrate
Platelets
>50 ×10<sup>9</sup>/L; >100 with TBI or ongoing bleeding
<50, or <100 with head injury
INR / PT ratio
>1.5 → plasma (slow signal — viscoelastic is faster)
Temperature
Always — warm everything, all the time
pH / base deficit
pH >7.2
Worsening base deficit means ongoing bleeding, not a bicarbonate problem
Potassium
<5.5 mmol/L
Rising with rapid transfusion of older units — especially in children
Blood pressure (pre-control)
Except TBI or spinal cord injury: SBP ≥110, MAP ≥80

blocks.html:
Reading viscoelastic tests quickly. The point of TEG/ROTEM here is not elegance — it is that each abnormality maps to one bag.

  • Prolonged R time (TEG) / CT (EXTEM) → not enough clotting factors → plasma (or PCC in the anticoagulated).
  • Narrow alpha angle, prolonged K / low FIBTEM A10 → not enough fibrinogen → cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate.
  • Low MA (TEG) / low EXTEM A10 with normal FIBTEM → not enough platelets → platelets.
  • LY30 >3% / increased maximum lysis → hyperfibrinolysis → TXA.

Permissive hypotension until hemorrhage is controlled: a clot formed at SBP 85 survives; the same clot is blown off at SBP 140. The exceptions are absolute — a brain or cord that is also injured needs perfusion pressure more than it needs a protected clot.

Crystalloid is not resuscitation. Keep it under 1 L before blood arrives, and ideally near zero. It dilutes clotting factors, worsens acidosis, drops the temperature, and raises pressure enough to displace clot — four harms, no benefit.

steps.title: Activate out loud, and name the person
steps.html: “I am activating massive transfusion. [Name], you are calling the blood bank.” Undirected instructions in a full room get executed by nobody. State the location, the patient identifier, and that this is an MTP activation.

steps.title: Assign the four jobs
steps.html: Blood bank liaison (the only person who talks to blood bank, and who keeps the runner moving) · Rapid infuser operator (does nothing else) · Scribe (units in, times, calcium doses, labs sent) · Team leader (source control and the decision to keep going). One person cannot hold two of these.

steps.title: Start uncrossmatched now, send the type and screen simultaneously
steps.html: Do not hold the first unit waiting for a crossmatch. Send the sample at the same moment the emergency-release blood is hung, so the switch to type-specific product is ready when the initial supply runs down.

steps.title: Give TXA and calcium with pack 1
steps.html: Both are time-sensitive and both are the things that get remembered at minute 40. Check the injury clock for the 3-hour TXA window before giving it.

steps.title: Warm everything
steps.html: Infuser warmer on and verified at temperature, forced-air blanket over whatever is not exposed, room heat up, wet clothing cut off and removed. Hypothermia here is iatrogenic and it is the leg of the lethal triad you have the most direct control over.

steps.title: Get labs at activation and every 30–60 minutes
steps.html: Blood gas with ionized calcium, CBC, fibrinogen, PT/INR, and viscoelastic if available. Fibrinogen specifically — it is not on a standard coagulation panel at many sites and it is the first thing to fail.

steps.title: Drive toward source control the whole time
steps.html: OR, interventional radiology, endoscopy, balloon tamponade, a binder, a tourniquet, uterotonics. Every round of product is a question about why the bleeding has not stopped. If the answer is “we are still waiting for the OR,” escalate that instead of hanging another unit.

steps.title: Deactivate explicitly, and return the cooler
steps.html: Call blood bank and say the protocol is off. Unopened coolers go back promptly — units held at the bedside past their window are destroyed, and a regional supply is finite. This step is skipped constantly.

rows: Product arrives but nothing is going in fast
Access is the limit — long, narrow catheters
Place a short large-bore peripheral or an 8.5 Fr introducer. Not a triple lumen.
Pack 1 is all red cells, no plasma
Plasma is still thawing
Expected. Ask whether pre-thawed plasma or LTOWB exists. Do not slow the red cells waiting.
Bleeding from every puncture site and mucosa
Established coagulopathy — usually fibrinogen and calcium
Cryoprecipitate and calcium now, do not wait for the panel. Send viscoelastic.
Pressure won't come up despite volume
Ongoing bleeding you have not found — or a non-hemorrhagic cause
Reassess the four spaces (chest, abdomen, pelvis/retroperitoneum, long bones and the floor). Rule out tension pneumothorax and tamponade — both mimic refractory hemorrhagic shock.
Sudden arrest mid-transfusion
Hyperkalemia or profound ionized hypocalcemia from rapid product delivery
Calcium immediately. Treat hyperkalemia. This is more common with older units, rapid central infusion, and children.
Widening QRS, peaked T waves
Hyperkalemia from stored red cells
Calcium, insulin/dextrose, consider washed or fresher units for continued transfusion.
Temperature falling despite a warmer
Warmer not at temperature, or bypassed by a side line
Verify the warmer is actually in circuit and the display is at target. Cover everything else.
Hypotension right after TXA
Pushed too fast
TXA goes over 10 minutes. Slow it.
Hypoxia and infiltrates within 6 h
TRALI or TACO
Supportive care and respiratory support; distinguish by volume status and response to diuresis. Report the reaction — it changes future product selection.
Blood bank says they are out
Regional supply limit reached

This is a command decision, not a clinical one: escalate to the blood bank medical director and consider transfer, damage-control surgery now rather than later, and an explicit goals-of-care conversation.

blocks.html:
• Hypothermia — worsens platelet function and enzyme kinetics. Largely iatrogenic and largely preventable.
  • Ionized hypocalcemia — citrate-driven; causes coagulopathy, hypotension, and arrest. The single most under-treated complication of massive transfusion.
  • Hyperkalemia — potassium leaks from stored red cells; risk scales with unit age, infusion rate, and inversely with patient size.
  • Dilutional coagulopathy — from crystalloid and from red-cell-heavy ratios.
  • Metabolic alkalosis — a late effect as citrate is metabolized to bicarbonate.
  • TRALI (within 6 h, non-cardiogenic infiltrates) and TACO (volume overload) — both present as post-transfusion hypoxia and are distinguished mainly by volume status.
  • Acute hemolytic reaction — rare with emergency-release O product; the real risk is a mislabeled sample. Two-person identity verification does not stop during a resuscitation.
  • Transfusion-associated immunomodulation and infection risk — dose-dependent, and a reason to stop when bleeding stops.
  • Abdominal compartment syndrome after large-volume resuscitation — measure bladder pressure if the abdomen becomes tense and oliguria or high airway pressures develop.

Three units in an hour is your trigger. Of all the scores, CAT+ is the one you can actually notice in real time.

Calcium with the first pack, every time. It is the most commonly omitted and most rapidly lethal deficiency in the whole protocol, and it is one syringe.

Check the clock before giving TXA. Within 3 hours it helps; beyond it, the trial data point the other way. Bleeding alone is not the indication — timing is.

One apheresis platelet equals six units. Miscount this and your “1:1:1” is a 6:6:6 — wildly over-plateleted — or you give six pooled bags thinking you are behind.

Fibrinogen fails first and is measured last. Order it explicitly; it is absent from many default coagulation panels.

Short and fat beats long and central. A 14 G peripheral moves more blood than a triple-lumen. If you want central, place an introducer sheath.

Keep the pressure low until the bleeding stops — unless the brain or cord is injured, where perfusion wins.

Every unit is a question about source control. The protocol is a bridge to an operation, an embolization, or a balloon. It is not a destination.

Deactivate and send the cooler back. Unglamorous, constantly forgotten, and the difference between a functioning regional blood supply and a depleted one.
